learningObjectives.title: Stalin's rule: collectivisation, purges and the Five-Year Plans

questions.q: Who was the ruler of Russia at the start of the period, overthrown in 1917?
options: Tsar Alexander III
Tsar Nicholas II
Tsar Peter the Great
Tsar Ivan IV
questions.explain: Nicholas II was the last Tsar of Russia and was forced to abdicate in March 1917.

questions.q: What name is given to the events of January 1905 when troops fired on peaceful protesters marching to the Winter Palace?
options: The July Days
Bloody Sunday
The Kornilov Affair
The October Days
questions.explain: On Bloody Sunday in January 1905 the Tsar's troops shot at peaceful marchers led by Father Gapon, sparking the 1905 Revolution.

questions.q: What did Nicholas II promise in the October Manifesto of 1905?
options: An elected parliament called the Duma
The abolition of serfdom
Withdrawal from the First World War
The redistribution of all noble land
questions.explain: The October Manifesto promised an elected Duma and civil rights, helping to calm the 1905 Revolution.

questions.q: Why did Rasputin's presence at court damage the reputation of the monarchy before 1917?
options: He publicly supported the Bolsheviks
He commanded the Russian army during defeats
He gained great influence over the Tsarina, fuelling rumours and scandal
He was a foreign spy working for Germany's government
questions.explain: Rasputin's influence over the Tsarina, linked to treating the heir's haemophilia, created scandal that undermined public trust in the royal family.

questions.q: Why was Nicholas II's decision in 1915 to take personal command of the army so damaging?
options: It left the Tsarina and Rasputin influencing government while he was blamed for defeats
It forced Russia to make peace with Germany
It gave Lenin control of the Duma
It caused the immediate collapse of the railways
questions.explain: By taking command Nicholas became personally associated with military failures while government at home was left weak and discredited.

questions.q: In which month and year did Nicholas II abdicate the throne?
options: October 1905
March 1917
November 1917
July 1918
questions.explain: Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917 (February by the old Russian calendar) following mass strikes and mutiny in Petrograd.

questions.q: A factory worker in Petrograd in early 1917 faces bread shortages, freezing fuel queues and joins mass strikes, while soldiers refuse to fire on crowds. These conditions most directly led to which outcome?
options: The abdication of the Tsar
The signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
The launch of the First Five-Year Plan
The victory of the Whites in the civil war
questions.explain: Food shortages, strikes and army mutiny in Petrograd in February/March 1917 forced Nicholas II to abdicate.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'dual power' that existed in Russia after the Tsar's abdication in 1917?
options: Power was shared between Germany and the Provisional Government
Power was split between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet
Power was divided between the Tsar and the Duma
Power was held jointly by Lenin and Trotsky
questions.explain: Authority was divided between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, weakening effective control of the country.

questions.q: Which slogan did Lenin use to win support after his return to Russia in April 1917?
options: Peace, Bread, Land
Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Blood, Toil and Tears
Workers of the World Unite
questions.explain: Lenin's slogan 'Peace, Bread, Land' promised an end to war, food and land redistribution, winning popular support for the Bolsheviks.

questions.q: A historian asks why the Bolsheviks were able to seize power in November 1917 with relatively little resistance. Which factor best explains this?
options: The unpopularity and weakness of the Provisional Government
The strong support of foreign armies for the Bolsheviks
The Tsar's decision to lead a counter-attack
The Bolsheviks' large majority in the Duma since 1905
questions.explain: The Provisional Government's failures, especially continuing the war, left it too weak and unpopular to resist the Bolshevik seizure of power.

questions.q: Why did the Provisional Government become deeply unpopular during 1917?
options: It abolished the Orthodox Church
It chose to continue fighting in the First World War
It handed all land to the nobility
It executed the Tsar without trial
questions.explain: The Provisional Government's decision to keep fighting the war worsened shortages and casualties, destroying its support.

questions.q: What did the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) achieve for Russia?
options: It brought Russia out of the First World War
It united the Reds and Whites
It gave Russia control of Poland
It ended collectivisation
questions.explain: By the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk the Bolsheviks made peace with Germany, taking Russia out of the war at the cost of large territories.

questions.q: Why was Trotsky important to the Bolshevik (Red) victory in the civil war?
options: He negotiated foreign loans from Britain
He organised and led the Red Army with great effectiveness
He controlled the White forces from within
He introduced the New Economic Policy
questions.explain: As Commissar for War, Trotsky built and led a disciplined Red Army that proved decisive in defeating the Whites.

questions.q: During the civil war a Bolshevik official forcibly seizes grain from peasants to feed the Red Army and the cities. This action is part of which policy?
options: War Communism
The New Economic Policy
Collectivisation
The October Manifesto
questions.explain: War Communism involved requisitioning grain from peasants and state control of the economy to sustain the Red war effort.

questions.q: Why were the Reds ultimately able to defeat the Whites in the civil war?
options: The Whites received no foreign help at all
The Reds held the central regions, railways and were united under one leadership
The Whites had far fewer soldiers throughout
The Reds made peace with all the White generals
questions.explain: Controlling the industrial centre and railways, and being unified under Bolshevik leadership, gave the Reds decisive advantages over the divided Whites.

questions.q: In which year did Lenin die, opening the struggle for leadership that Stalin eventually won?
questions.explain: Lenin died in 1924, after which Stalin gradually outmanoeuvred rivals such as Trotsky to gain control.

questions.q: The first Five-Year Plan, launched in 1928, concentrated above all on which goal?
options: Expanding heavy industry
Increasing exports of luxury goods
Rebuilding the Tsarist navy
Encouraging private trade
questions.explain: The first Five-Year Plan prioritised heavy industry such as coal, iron, steel and electricity to modernise the USSR rapidly.

questions.q: What was the main aim of Stalin's policy of collectivisation of agriculture?
options: To return land to the nobility
To merge small farms into large collective farms to boost output and feed the towns
To reduce the size of the Red Army
To encourage peasants to own private plots
questions.explain: Collectivisation combined peasant holdings into large collective farms (kolkhozes) to increase grain output and supply the growing industrial cities.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of Stalin's purges and show trials in the 1930s?
options: To raise industrial wages
To eliminate real and suspected opponents and secure Stalin's total control
To expand Russia's borders westwards
To end the Five-Year Plans
questions.explain: The Great Purge removed party rivals, army officers and ordinary citizens through executions and labour camps, cementing Stalin's dictatorship.

questions.q: A peasant in 1930 who owns several cows, hires labour and resists joining a collective farm is most likely to be labelled and persecuted as which of the following?
options: A kulak
A commissar
A White general
A Menshevik
questions.explain: Better-off peasants who resisted collectivisation were branded kulaks and were dispossessed, deported or killed under Stalin's campaign.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE History (0470) syllabus; Depth Study: Russia 1905-41
